why: #453. A lambda with a receiver — `with(x) { }`, `x.apply { }`, `x.run { }`, `buildString { }` — puts that receiver's members ahead of the enclosing class's, and a bare call inside one was being resolved to a same-named member of the enclosing class. On the Android validation app that minted 17 self-loops, a Gradle convention plugin's `apply(target: Project)` calling itself for every `apply(\"plugin-id\")` written inside `with(pluginManager) { }`. Kotlin's rule is innermost receiver first, then outward, then the enclosing class; this front-end cannot show what a receiver declares, so inside a recognised receiver lambda it **refuses** the enclosing-member reading and never redirects the call to a receiver — the rule can only remove an edge. The labels are Kotlin's true answers regardless: where the refusal gives one up (`viaReceiver`, `fallsBack`) it is a known gap, not an omission. The four `control*` functions pin what must not change: `run`/`let`/`also` do not change the receiver, and a top-level import keeps resolving.

excluded: java:org.gradle.api.Project and java:org.gradle.api.plugins.PluginManager are external, imported and never declared here, so they stay out of the node ratio per corpus/README.md; the IMPORTS edges to them count, and so do the CALLS edges to `PluginManager.apply` (as `known_gaps`).

Calls into the Kotlin standard library are not labelled: `with`, `run`, `let`, `also`, `buildString`, and `render`'s `append("header")`, whose true target is `append` on the builder's `kotlin.text.StringBuilder`. Unlike Gradle's `PluginManager` above — an ordinary imported class with one id, labelled as a known gap — that receiver is a Kotlin typealias whose id (`kotlin.text.StringBuilder` or the JVM's `java.lang.StringBuilder`) this vocabulary has never decided, and the front-end has no model of the standard library; that is the decision `scope_functions` records for `let`/`run`/`use`. Refusing the fabricated `Report.append` is what this case measures.

What this case cannot settle, and does not pretend to: inside `with(pluginManager) { log("applied") }` the call is labelled `java:app.util.log` because Gradle's `PluginManager` declares no `log`. That is knowledge of Gradle, not of this tree. A library receiver that *did* declare a same-named member would hide an imported or top-level function the same way, and the front-end keeps the top-level reading there because it cannot read the library (#453; `_ReceiverCall` in `kotlin_extractor.py` states the limit). For a repo-declared receiver the case does not arise: its members are checked first (`viaReceiver`).
